verses.text: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Haven’t I seen Jesus Christ, our Lord? Aren’t you my work in the Lord?
If to others I am not an apostle, yet at least I am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
My defense to those who examine me is this.
Have we no right to eat and to drink?
Have we no right to take along a wife who is a believer, even as the rest of the apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?
Or have only Barnabas and I no right to not work?
What soldier ever serves at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard, and doesn’t eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock, and doesn’t drink from the flock’s milk?
Do I speak these things according to the ways of men? Or doesn’t the law also say the same thing?
For it is written in the law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.”  Is it for the oxen that God cares,
or does he say it assuredly for our sake? Yes, it was written for our sake, because he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope should partake of his hope.
If we sowed to you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we reap your fleshly things?
If others partake of this right over you, don’t we yet more? Nevertheless we did not use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.
Don’t you know that those who serve around sacred things eat from the things of the temple, and those who wait on the altar have their portion with the altar?
Even so the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Good News should live from the Good News.
But I have used none of these things, and I don’t write these things that it may be done so in my case; for I would rather die, than that anyone should make my boasting void.
For if I preach the Good News, I have nothing to boast about; for necessity is laid on me; but woe is to me, if I don’t preach the Good News.
For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward. But if not of my own will, I have a stewardship entrusted to me.
What then is my reward? That, when I preach the Good News, I may present the Good News of Christ without charge, so as not to abuse my authority in the Good News.
For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.
To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law;
to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law.
To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.
Now I do this for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it.
Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, that you may win.
Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.
I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air,
but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.

footnotes.content: Paul opens his whole defense with questions—not defensive, but inviting: *Have you forgotten who I am?* He was no second-rate teacher; he'd seen the risen Jesus himself and the work of the Spirit in Corinth was his living proof. Sometimes the gentlest confidence comes from resting in what God has already done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His apostolic seal was written in their changed hearts. Even if the world doubted, Corinth itself was the proof—brokenness healed, idolatry turned to worship. When you wonder if your faithfulness matters, remember: the Gospel leaves marks that can't be erased.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul braces himself. This isn't casual chatter—there are people examining his life, his choices, maybe his motives. Yet instead of anger, he offers patient reason. A true leader doesn't dodge hard questions; he answers them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He starts with the basics: an apostle's right to be fed and cared for. Not extravagance—just the simple truth that a worker deserves food. Paul isn't pleading poverty; he's establishing what is *just*, before he explains why he chose differently.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He mentions Cephas—Peter—taking a believing wife with him in his travels, and the Lord's brothers doing the same. These weren't secret doubters; they were the Jerusalem pillars. Paul's point: if the greatest apostles took support from the churches, surely he could too. Yet he chose not to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barnabas stands beside Paul in this sacrifice—his partner, his fellow laborer, doing the same hard thing: working with their own hands while preaching. There's quiet fellowship in shared hardship, a bond that money alone can never create.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He calls three witnesses from common life—the soldier, the vineyard keeper, the shepherd—each drawing their living from what they tend. It's the logic of work itself, written into creation: care earns sustenance. Paul appeals not to sentiment but to the order of things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He pushes back gently: *You don't think I'm inventing this from human reasoning, do you?* The Law itself upholds what he's saying. Paul isn't out of step with Scripture—he's walking in it, even when it would be easier not to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He quotes Deuteronomy 25:4 about the muzzled ox—a law that seems small until you see its reach. God cares about the working animal's hunger. If the Law guards the ox's belly, surely it guards the worker's plate. The command reaches forward to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Moses's ox law wasn't really *for* oxen—it was written for the one who labors in hope. The Law teaches God's heart: He sees the plowman's sweat, the reaper's weariness, and He means their labor to feed them. Trust reaches all the way down to work itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fair question: *If we've given you spiritual treasure, can't we ask for bread?* Surely the supply should match the gift. Paul has sown Gospel seed; harvest is reasonable. Yet he'll show why he refuses it anyway—not because it's unjust, but for a deeper love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Other teachers *did* use their right to eat at Corinth's table—and Paul honors that. But for himself, he bore all things rather than set a stumbling block before the Gospel. Love sometimes means laying down what you deserve, because something larger than your comfort is at stake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He brings the temple priests forward as witnesses: those who serve holy things eat from holy things—it's the pattern of Scripture itself. A priest didn't starve for serving God; the altar provided. The principle is ancient and right. Paul isn't arguing against it; he's choosing to set it aside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord *ordained* that Gospel workers live from the Gospel. This isn't Paul's invention or his opinion—it's Christ's command. Yet somehow grace flows deeper than rules. The permission is real; the choice to forgo it is realer still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Paul's heart shows: *I have used none of these things.* Not from shame or false poverty, but from a white-hot conviction—he'd rather die than let anyone say he preached for money. His boasting is in Christ alone, untainted by even the suspicion of self-interest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He strips away all pretense: *Necessity is laid on me; woe is me if I don't preach!* This is no career choice. The Gospel seized Paul on the Damascus road and won't let him go. He preaches because he *must*, not because it's clever or safe or profitable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he chose this calling freely, he'd earn a reward—the pleasure of knowing he chose well. But he didn't choose it; it chose him. A stewardship has been entrusted to him, like a household servant given keys and responsibility. The servant doesn't brag about obeying; they obey.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So what *is* Paul's reward? That he can preach Christ *without charge*, making the Good News absolutely free—no price, no debt, no obligation. That's his joy: offering what's most precious without any shadow of self-gain. The Gospel tastes purest when nothing taints it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A turning point: Paul now describes the shape his freedom takes—he made himself a servant *to all*, putting on others' constraints like borrowed garments. True freedom doesn't hoard itself; it spends itself on others' gain. That's the paradox Paul has learned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To Jews he became as a Jew, honoring their law and hope. Not fake—a real entering-in, a real listening. Paul didn't strip culture to preach Christ; he wrapped himself in others' robes so they'd see the Gospel *in* their own language. Humility is the translator's art.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To the lawless he became lawless—not in sin, but in meeting them where they stood. Yet even then: *not without law toward God, but under law toward Christ.* Paul never forgets his anchor. He bends his shoulder to every door, but his heart stays tethered to Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To the weak, he became weak—not condescension, but solidarity. *I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.* It's the grammar of love: losing yourself to find others. A lifelong apprenticeship in the art of reaching hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why does Paul do all this? *For the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it.* Not to boast or to build a name, but to share in the Gospel's power himself—to be caught up, changed, transformed by the same grace he offers. He's not above it; he's inside it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Paul shifts to the race—a Corinthian would know the games, the stadium, the runners straining. *Run like that, that you may win.* Not everyone finishes; only one takes the prize. Paul is calling believers to the same intensity, the same willingness to exhaust themselves for something that lasts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every athlete masters their body—they deny themselves to condition themselves. But for what? A wreath that wilts. How much more should we discipline ourselves for a crown that never fades? The racers show us the shape of true effort, even if they're running for a perishable prize.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in *not aimlessly* and *not beating the air*—Paul's picture speaks to our scattered age. He ran with aim, threw every punch with purpose, wasted nothing on shadow-boxing. We hear him asking: where is your aim? What is your fight really for?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The final word: *I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.* Paul takes his own advice—he runs hard, disciplines himself, keeps vigilance. Preaching truth means living it, or the words ring hollow. The finish line demands we run all the way through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
